## Introduction

Nepalese community in the United States continues to grow, with strong roots in Nepal- a South Asian Country known for the Himalayas and Mount Everest. In the United States, have built communities while keeping their language, culture, and traditions alive. New York City, especially Queens, has become an important place for this community.

This atlas entry looks at where Nepalese Americans live, starting with neighborhoods in New York City and then looking at their presence across the United States.Using the 2024 American Community Survey (ACS) 5-year estimates, NYC neighborhood boundaries, and PLUTO building data, the report combines Census findings and interactive maps to tell the story of where Nepalese communities are concentrated, how they are distributed across different cities, and some unexpected patterns in their geographic distribution.


## Data Acquisition

This report uses data from the 2024 American Community Survey (ACS), New York City's Neighborhood Tabulation Areas (NTAs), and PLUTO building data to explore population and geographic patterns. 

The ACS provides populations estimates including Nepalese population.I used the ACS 5-year estimates from 2020 to 2024 instead of the 1-year estimates because they provide better coverage for studying smaller communities, including Nepalese Americans. 

The datasets were downloaded and saved locally to avoid repeated downloads and make the analysis easier to reproduce.

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
library(tidyverse)
library(tidycensus)
library(sf)
library(httr2)
library(fs)
library(gt)

options(tigris_use_cache = TRUE)

DATA_DIR <- fs::path("data", "mp03")
fs::dir_create(DATA_DIR, recurse = TRUE)

# Nepalese in table B02018 (Asian alone or in any combination, by group).
# Checked for 2024 ACS-1 and ACS-5: B02018_024 = "South Asian: Nepalese".
# NOTE: this number changed between years (it was B02018_016 in 2021),
# so re-check it if you switch to a different year.
GROUP_VAR <- "B02018_024"
ACS_YEAR  <- 2024
```

```{r}
#| label: acs-cache-helper
#| include: false
# Same caching idea as MP02: only hit the API if the file isn't saved yet.
# To refresh (e.g. after adding variables), delete the matching .rds file.

get_acs_cached <- function(file_name, ...){
    file_path <- fs::path(DATA_DIR, paste0(file_name, ".rds"))

    if(!fs::file_exists(file_path)){
        result <- get_acs(...)
        saveRDS(result, file_path)
    }

    readRDS(file_path)
}
```

### Metro Area (CBSA) Population

```{r}
#| label: task1-cbsa
# Task 1: total population and Nepalese population for every metro area (ACS-5; ACS-1 suppresses Nepalese counts)
cbsa_pop <- get_acs_cached(
    "cbsa_nepalese_acs5",
    geography = "cbsa",
    variables = c(total = "B01003_001", nepalese = GROUP_VAR),
    year      = ACS_YEAR,
    survey    = "acs5",
    output    = "wide"
) |>
    mutate(nepalese_share = nepaleseE / totalE)

# Full B02018 table for every metro, used for the ancestry-mix question (Q5)
cbsa_asian_groups <- get_acs_cached(
    "cbsa_b02018_acs5",
    geography = "cbsa",
    table     = "B02018",
    year      = ACS_YEAR,
    survey    = "acs5"
)

# Variable labels, so B02018_0xx codes can be turned into group names
acs1_vars <- {
    f <- fs::path(DATA_DIR, "acs5_variables.rds")
    if(!fs::file_exists(f)) saveRDS(load_variables(ACS_YEAR, "acs5"), f)
    readRDS(f)
}

# National total, used for the "share of all US Nepalese" question (Q6)
us_pop <- get_acs_cached(
    "us_nepalese_acs5",
    geography = "us",
    variables = c(total = "B01003_001", nepalese = GROUP_VAR),
    year      = ACS_YEAR,
    survey    = "acs5",
    output    = "wide"
)
```

Core-Based Statistical Areas (CBSAs) are geographic regions that include cities and their surrounding areas to compare Nepalese population patterns across different areas of the United States.

### NYC Census Tract Population

```{r}
#| label: task2-tracts
# Task 2: same variables at tract level for the 5 NYC counties (ACS-5), with shapes
NYC_COUNTIES <- c("New York", "Kings", "Queens", "Bronx", "Richmond")

nyc_tracts <- get_acs_cached(
    "nyc_tracts_nepalese_acs5",
    geography = "tract",
    state     = "NY",
    county    = NYC_COUNTIES,
    variables = c(total = "B01003_001", nepalese = GROUP_VAR),
    year      = ACS_YEAR,
    survey    = "acs5",
    output    = "wide",
    geometry  = TRUE
)
```

Census tracts are small geographic areas defined by the US Census Bureau to study population patterns.Population data for census tracts were used across all five boroughs of New York City to identify where Nepalese residents live and how their population is distributed across different parts of the city.

### NYC Neighborhood Tabulation Areas

```{r}
#| label: task3-nta
# Task 3: download, unzip and read the 2020 NTA shapefile (not via tidycensus)
load_nyc_nta <- function(){
    NTA_URL  <- "https://s-media.nyc.gov/agencies/dcp/assets/files/zip/data-tools/bytes/neighborhood-tabulation-areas/nynta2020_26c.zip"
    zip_file <- fs::path(DATA_DIR, "nynta2020.zip")

    if(!fs::file_exists(zip_file)){
        request(NTA_URL) |>
            req_headers(
                `User-Agent` = "Mozilla/5.0 (Macintosh; Intel Mac OS X 10.15; rv:149.0) Gecko/20100101 Firefox/149.0"
            ) |>
            req_retry(max_tries = 4) |>
            req_perform(path = zip_file)
    }

    # Stop early if the download isn't a real zip (e.g. a web page)
    # (every real zip file starts with the letters "PK")
    zip_ok <- identical(readBin(zip_file, "raw", 2), charToRaw("PK"))
    if(!zip_ok){
        fs::file_delete(zip_file)
        stop("NTA download is not a valid zip file. Check NTA_URL.")
    }

    shp_file <- fs::dir_ls(DATA_DIR, recurse = TRUE, glob = "*nynta2020*.shp")

    if(length(shp_file) == 0){
        unzip(zip_file, exdir = DATA_DIR, unzip = "unzip")  # macOS system unzip
        shp_file <- fs::dir_ls(DATA_DIR, recurse = TRUE, glob = "*nynta2020*.shp")
    }

    st_read(shp_file[1], quiet = TRUE) |>
        # NTAType: 0 = residential neighborhood; other codes are parks,
        # airports, cemeteries etc. Kept so those can be filtered out later.
        select(BoroName, NTA2020, NTAName, NTAType)
}

nyc_nta <- load_nyc_nta()
```

Neighborhood Tabulation Areas (NTAs) is used to study population patterns at the neighborhood level. These boundaries group smaller census tracts into larger neighborhoods, making it easier to compare different areas.


### Aggregating Tracts to Neighborhoods

```{r}
#| label: task4-tract-to-nta
# Task 4: give each tract the NTA it overlaps most, then add tracts up per NTA.
# 2020 NTAs are built from whole 2020 tracts, so largest = TRUE is a clean match.
nyc_tracts <- st_transform(nyc_tracts, st_crs(nyc_nta))

tract_to_nta <- nyc_tracts |>
    st_join(nyc_nta, join = st_intersects, largest = TRUE)

nta_pop <- tract_to_nta |>
    st_drop_geometry() |>
    group_by(NTA2020) |>
    summarize(
        total    = sum(totalE, na.rm = TRUE),
        nepalese = sum(nepaleseE, na.rm = TRUE),
        .groups  = "drop"
    )

nta_data <- nyc_nta |>
    left_join(nta_pop, by = "NTA2020") |>
    mutate(nepalese_share = nepalese / total)
```

I grouped census tracts into their matching NTAs and added up their population estimates. This helps me compare the total population and Nepalese population in different NYC neighborhoods.

### NYC PLUTO (Tax Lot Data)

```{r}
#| label: task5-pluto
# Task 5: page through the PLUTO API and save one CSV (cached like MP02)
load_pluto <- function(){
    PLUTO_FILE <- fs::path(DATA_DIR, "pluto.csv")

    if(!fs::file_exists(PLUTO_FILE)){
        BASE_URL  <- "https://data.cityofnewyork.us/resource/64uk-42ks.csv"
        # Only the columns needed later
        PLUTO_COLS <- c("bbl", "borough", "bct2020", "landuse",
                        "lotarea", "bldgarea", "comarea", "resarea",
                        "officearea", "retailarea",
                        "unitsres", "unitstotal", "numfloors")
        PAGE_SIZE <- 50000
        offset    <- 0
        pages     <- list()

        repeat {
            page <- request(BASE_URL) |>
                req_url_query(
                    `$select` = paste(PLUTO_COLS, collapse = ","),
                    `$order`  = "bbl",          # fixed order so pages don't overlap
                    `$limit`  = PAGE_SIZE,
                    `$offset` = offset
                ) |>
                req_retry(max_tries = 4) |>
                req_perform() |>
                resp_body_string() |>
                read_csv(col_types = cols(.default = col_character()))

            if(nrow(page) == 0) break
            pages[[length(pages) + 1]] <- page
            if(nrow(page) < PAGE_SIZE) break
            offset <- offset + PAGE_SIZE
        }

        bind_rows(pages) |> write_csv(PLUTO_FILE)
    }

    read_csv(
        PLUTO_FILE,
        col_types = cols(
            bbl = col_character(), borough = col_character(),
            bct2020 = col_character(), landuse = col_character(),
            .default = col_double()
        )
    )
}

pluto <- load_pluto()

# bct2020 = borough digit + 6-digit tract (e.g. 1000100).
# Convert to the Census GEOID (e.g. 36061000100) so PLUTO can join to tracts.
BORO_TO_COUNTY <- c("1" = "061", "2" = "005", "3" = "047", "4" = "081", "5" = "085")

pluto <- pluto |>
    mutate(
        bct2020 = str_remove(bct2020, "\\.0+$"),
        GEOID   = paste0("36",
                         BORO_TO_COUNTY[str_sub(bct2020, 1, 1)],
                         str_sub(bct2020, 2))
    )

# One row per tract with building totals, for the EDA questions
tract_buildings <- pluto |>
    filter(!is.na(bct2020)) |>
    group_by(GEOID) |>
    summarize(
        office_area = sum(officearea, na.rm = TRUE),
        res_area    = sum(resarea,    na.rm = TRUE),
        com_area    = sum(comarea,    na.rm = TRUE),
        bldg_area   = sum(bldgarea,   na.rm = TRUE),
        res_units   = sum(unitsres,   na.rm = TRUE),
        max_floors  = if (all(is.na(numfloors))) NA_real_ else max(numfloors, na.rm = TRUE),
        .groups     = "drop"
    )
```

PLUTO provides information about NYC properties, including residential units, office space, commercial space and building height. This information helps explore how housing and buildings relate to population patterns.


## Data Validation and Quality Checks
```{r}
#| label: data-check
# Quick sanity checks: run these and look at the numbers before moving on
tibble(
    check = c("Metros", "NYC tracts", "NTAs", "PLUTO lots",
              "PLUTO tracts matched to Census tracts"),
    value = c(nrow(cbsa_pop), nrow(nyc_tracts), nrow(nyc_nta), nrow(pluto),
              sum(tract_buildings$GEOID %in% nyc_tracts$GEOID))
) |>
    gt()
```

I checked the number of records in each dataset and compared the PLUTO census tract IDs with the Census data to find any missing or unmatched records before starting the analysis.


## Exploratory Data Analysis

This section explores population patterns, housing, and building characteristics across New York City, along with the distribution of Nepalese communities throughout the United States. Using tables, charts, and maps, different areas are compared and interesting patterns were highlighted. 

```{r}
#| label: eda-prep
library(scales)

# One row per NYC tract: Census population + its NTA + PLUTO building totals
tract_lookup <- tract_to_nta |>
    st_drop_geometry() |>
    select(GEOID, tract_name = NAME, NTA2020, NTAName, BoroName,
           pop = totalE, nepalese = nepaleseE)

tract_full <- tract_lookup |>
    left_join(tract_buildings, by = "GEOID")
```

### Q1.Which NYC census tract has the most office floor area?

```{r}
#| label: tbl-q1-office
q1 <- tract_full |>
    slice_max(office_area, n = 5) |>
    select(tract_name, NTAName, BoroName, office_area)

top_office <- q1 |> slice(1)

q1 |>
    gt() |>
    cols_label(tract_name = "Census Tract", NTAName = "Neighborhood",
               BoroName = "Borough", office_area = "Office Floor Area (sq ft)") |>
    fmt_number(office_area, decimals = 0) |>
    tab_header(title = "NYC Tracts with the Most Office Space")
```

According to PLUTO data, `r top_office$tract_name` in `r top_office$NTAName`, `r top_office$BoroName`, has the highest office floor area in New York City, with approximately `r scales::comma(round(top_office$office_area))` square feet. This may be because the area is a major business center with many large office buildings. The result shows how office space is concentrated in certain parts of the city.


### Q2. Which NYC NTA has the most residential units?

```{r}
#| label: q2-units
nta_units <- tract_full |>
    group_by(NTA2020, NTAName, BoroName) |>
    summarize(res_units = sum(res_units, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") |>
    arrange(desc(res_units))

top_units_nta <- nta_units |> slice(1)
```

The neighborhood with the most residential units is `r top_units_nta$NTAName` in `r top_units_nta$BoroName`, with approximately `r scales::comma(round(top_units_nta$res_units))` units. This suggests that the area has a large amount of housing, possibly because of its size or the presence of apartment buildings. However, having more residential units does not necessarily mean having the highest population.

### Q3. Which census tract has the highest population per residential space?

```{r}
#| label: tbl-q3-density
# Small denominators give silly results (e.g. a tract with 2 apartments and
# a big dorm or prison), so only tracts with a real amount of housing count.
q3 <- tract_full |>
    filter(pop >= 500, res_area >= 50000, res_units >= 50) |>
    mutate(
        pop_per_1000_sqft = pop / res_area * 1000,
        pop_per_unit      = pop / res_units
    )

q3_sqft <- q3 |> slice_max(pop_per_1000_sqft, n = 5) |>
    mutate(measure = "People per 1,000 sq ft of residential space")
q3_unit <- q3 |> slice_max(pop_per_unit, n = 5) |>
    mutate(measure = "People per residential unit")

same_top_tract <- q3_sqft$GEOID[1] == q3_unit$GEOID[1]

bind_rows(q3_sqft, q3_unit) |>
    select(measure, tract_name, NTAName, pop, pop_per_1000_sqft, pop_per_unit) |>
    gt(groupname_col = "measure") |>
    cols_label(tract_name = "Census Tract", NTAName = "Neighborhood",
               pop = "Population", pop_per_1000_sqft = "per 1,000 sq ft",
               pop_per_unit = "per unit") |>
    fmt_number(pop, decimals = 0) |>
    fmt_number(c(pop_per_1000_sqft, pop_per_unit), decimals = 2) |>
    tab_header(title = "Most Densely Housed NYC Tracts, Two Ways")
```

I compared population density using two measures: people per 1,000 square feet of residential space and people per residential unit. The results `r if (same_top_tract) "identify the same census tract as the highest under both measures" else "identify different census tracts as the highest under each measure"`. I excluded tracts with fewer than 500 residents, 50 housing units, or 50,000 square feet of residential space to avoid misleading results from very small amounts of housing.


### Q4. Which five metro areas outside NYC have the highest Nepalese population share?

```{r}
#| label: tbl-q4-share
q4 <- cbsa_pop |>
    filter(!str_detect(NAME, "New York-Newark"), !is.na(nepaleseE)) |>
    slice_max(nepalese_share, n = 5) |>
    select(NAME, totalE, nepaleseE, nepaleseM, nepalese_share)

q4 |>
    gt() |>
    cols_label(NAME = "Metro Area", totalE = "Total Population",
               nepaleseE = "Nepalese", nepaleseM = "Margin of Error (±)",
               nepalese_share = "Nepalese Share") |>
    fmt_number(c(totalE, nepaleseE, nepaleseM), decimals = 0) |>
    fmt_percent(nepalese_share, decimals = 2) |>
    tab_header(title = "Metros (Outside NYC) with the Largest Nepalese Share")
```

The five areas with the highest estimated Nepalese population shares outside New York City are shown in the table. `r q4$NAME[1]` ranks first, with Nepalese residents making up approximately `r scales::percent(q4$nepalese_share[1], accuracy = 0.01)` of its population. This suggests that Nepalese communities may be particularly concentrated in some smaller urban areas. However, estimates for small populations can have large margins of error, so these rankings should be interpreted carefully.


### Q5. What is the distribution of Asian ancestry groups in another large metro area?

```{r}
#| label: fig-q5-ancestry
# Default: the non-NYC metro with the most Nepalese residents.
# You can replace this with any metro name from cbsa_pop$NAME.
COMPARISON_METRO <- cbsa_pop |>
    filter(!str_detect(NAME, "New York-Newark"), !is.na(nepaleseE)) |>
    slice_max(nepaleseE, n = 1) |>
    pull(NAME)

# Turn labels like "Estimate!!Total Groups Tallied:!!South Asian:!!Nepalese"
# into a broad region ("South Asian") and keep only the bottom-level rows,
# so nothing is counted twice.
b02018_labels <- acs1_vars |>
    filter(str_starts(name, "B02018_")) |>
    transmute(
        variable = name,
        depth    = str_count(label, "!!"),
        region   = str_remove(str_split_i(label, "!!", 3), ":$"),
        is_header = str_ends(label, ":")
    ) |>
    filter(depth >= 2, !is_header)

q5 <- cbsa_asian_groups |>
    filter(NAME == COMPARISON_METRO) |>
    inner_join(b02018_labels, by = "variable") |>
    group_by(region) |>
    summarize(people = sum(estimate, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")

ggplot(q5, aes(x = people, y = fct_reorder(region, people))) +
    geom_col(fill = "#2a7f8f") +
    scale_x_continuous(labels = comma) +
    labs(
        title    = paste("Asian Ancestry Groups in", COMPARISON_METRO),
        subtitle = "ACS 2024 5-year; people reporting more than one group are counted in each",
        x = "People", y = NULL
    ) +
    theme_minimal()
```

I selected `r COMPARISON_METRO` to explore the distribution of Asian population groups outside New York City. The chart compares the estimated populations of different groups, with `r q5$region[which.max(q5$people)]` having the largest total among the categories displayed. This shows that Asian communities in the metro area come from different backgrounds and are not evenly distributed across groups. People reporting multiple identities may be counted in more than one category.

### Q6. What share of Nepalese Americans live in New York and other major metro areas?

```{r}
#| label: tbl-q6-us-share
us_nepalese <- us_pop$nepaleseE

q6 <- cbsa_pop |>
    filter(!is.na(nepaleseE)) |>
    slice_max(nepaleseE, n = 10) |>
    mutate(share_of_us = nepaleseE / us_nepalese) |>
    select(NAME, nepaleseE, share_of_us)

ny_share    <- q6 |> filter(str_detect(NAME, "New York-Newark")) |> pull(share_of_us)
top10_share <- sum(q6$share_of_us)

q6 |>
    gt() |>
    cols_label(NAME = "Metro Area", nepaleseE = "Nepalese Residents",
               share_of_us = "Share of All US Nepalese") |>
    fmt_number(nepaleseE, decimals = 0) |>
    fmt_percent(share_of_us, decimals = 1) |>
    tab_header(title = "Ten Metros with the Most Nepalese Residents")
```

According to the 2024 ACS 5-year estimates, approximately `r scales::comma(us_nepalese)` people identify as Nepalese across the United States. The New York–Newark metro area accounts for about `r scales::percent(ny_share, accuracy = 0.1)` of this population, while the ten largest Nepalese-population metro areas together account for `r scales::percent(top10_share, accuracy = 0.1)`. This shows how much of the Nepalese population is concentrated in major urban areas, while others live outside these leading metros.

### Q7. Is there a relationship between population and housing?

```{r}
#| label: fig-q7-pop-housing
q7 <- tract_full |> filter(pop > 0, res_units > 0)
pop_unit_cor <- cor(q7$pop, q7$res_units)

ggplot(q7, aes(x = res_units, y = pop)) +
    geom_point(alpha = 0.25, size = 0.8) +
    geom_smooth(aes(color = "Straight line"), method = "lm", se = FALSE) +
    geom_smooth(aes(color = "Flexible curve"), method = "loess", se = FALSE) +
    scale_x_continuous(labels = comma) +
    scale_y_continuous(labels = comma) +
    scale_color_manual(values = c("Straight line" = "#d1495b",
                                  "Flexible curve" = "#2a7f8f")) +
    labs(title = "Population vs. Residential Units, NYC Census Tracts",
         x = "Residential units (PLUTO)", y = "Population (ACS 2024 5-year)",
         color = NULL) +
    theme_minimal() +
    theme(legend.position = "top")
```

The scatter plot shows how population changes with the number of residential units across NYC census tracts. The correlation is `r round(pop_unit_cor, 2)`, indicating `r if (pop_unit_cor >= 0.7) "a strong positive relationship" else if (pop_unit_cor >= 0.4) "a moderate positive relationship" else if (pop_unit_cor >= 0) "a weak positive relationship" else "a negative relationship"` between housing units and population. However, the points do not necessarily follow a perfect straight line because household sizes, building occupancy, and housing types vary across neighborhoods.

### Q8. Which NTAs have the tallest buildings?

```{r}
#| label: tbl-q8-floors
q8 <- pluto |>
    filter(!is.na(numfloors), numfloors > 0) |>
    inner_join(tract_lookup |> select(GEOID, NTA2020, NTAName, BoroName),
               by = "GEOID") |>
    group_by(NTA2020, NTAName, BoroName) |>
    summarize(
        max_floors    = max(numfloors),
        median_floors = median(numfloors),
        .groups = "drop"
    ) |>
    slice_max(max_floors, n = 10)

q8 |>
    select(-NTA2020) |>
    gt() |>
    cols_label(NTAName = "Neighborhood", BoroName = "Borough",
               max_floors = "Tallest Building (floors)",
               median_floors = "Typical Building (median floors)") |>
    fmt_number(c(max_floors, median_floors), decimals = 0) |>
    tab_header(title = "NYC Neighborhoods with the Tallest Buildings")
```

Based on PLUTO data, `r q8$NTAName[1]` in `r q8$BoroName[1]` has the tallest recorded building among the neighborhoods in the table, reaching `r scales::comma(q8$max_floors[1])` floors. Areas with very tall buildings may have more commercial activity or high-rise residential developments. However, the tallest building does not represent the typical building height in a neighborhood, so the table also includes median floors for comparison.

### Q9. How does population density vary across NYC?

```{r}
#| label: fig-q9-density-map
tract_density <- nyc_tracts |>
    mutate(
        area_sqmi = as.numeric(units::set_units(st_area(geometry), "mi^2")),
        density   = if_else(totalE > 0, totalE / area_sqmi, NA_real_)
    )

ggplot(tract_density) +
    geom_sf(aes(fill = density), color = NA) +
    scale_fill_viridis_c(trans = "log10", labels = comma,
                         na.value = "grey85", name = "People per\nsq mile") +
    labs(title = "Population Density by Census Tract",
         subtitle = "ACS 2024 5-year; grey = no residents (parks, airports)") +
    theme_void()
```

The map shows how population density differs across New York City's census tracts, measured in people per square mile. Darker areas represent higher population density, while lighter areas have fewer people per square mile. These differences may reflect variations in housing, land use, and residential development. The map also helps identify areas where residents live close together compared with less densely populated parts of the city.

### Q10. How many New Yorkers live in primarily commercial areas?

```{r}
#| label: q10-commercial
# My definition (you decide!): a tract is "primarily commercial" if at least
# half of its building floor area is commercial (PLUTO comarea / bldgarea).
COMMERCIAL_CUTOFF <- 0.5

q10 <- tract_full |>
    filter(bldg_area > 0) |>
    mutate(com_share = com_area / bldg_area,
           primarily_commercial = com_share >= COMMERCIAL_CUTOFF)

commercial_tracts <- sum(q10$primarily_commercial)
commercial_pop    <- sum(q10$pop[q10$primarily_commercial], na.rm = TRUE)
commercial_pct    <- commercial_pop / sum(q10$pop, na.rm = TRUE)
```

I defined a primarily commercial census tract as an area where at least 50% of the building floor space is used for commercial purposes. Based on this definition, `r scales::comma(commercial_tracts)` census tracts are primarily commercial, with approximately `r scales::comma(commercial_pop)` residents, representing `r scales::percent(commercial_pct, accuracy = 0.1)` of the population in the analyzed tracts. However, some of these areas may also contain residential buildings, so this definition is only an approximate measure of commercial land use.

## Beyond Ancestry: Birthplace and Income

Beyond identifying where Nepalese Americans live, this section explores their birthplace and the income levels of the neighborhoods where they live. Birthplace data helps us understand how many Nepalese residents were born in Nepal, while neighborhood income data provides a general picture of the economic conditions in these areas. Together, these findings help us better understand the Nepalese community in New York City beyond population numbers alone.

### Birthplace: How Many Nepalese Americans Are Immigrants?

```{r}
#| label: ec2-nepal-born
# Extra Credit #2a: how many people were born in Nepal (table B05006)?
# The Nepal line number in B05006 changes between years, so find it by
# its label instead of hardcoding it. Stops with an error if not found.
NEPAL_BORN_VAR <- acs1_vars |>
    filter(str_starts(name, "B05006_"), str_detect(label, "!!Nepal$")) |>
    pull(name)
stopifnot(length(NEPAL_BORN_VAR) == 1)

nepal_born_cbsa <- get_acs_cached(
    "cbsa_nepal_born_acs5",
    geography = "cbsa",
    variables = c(nepal_born = NEPAL_BORN_VAR),
    year = ACS_YEAR, survey = "acs5", output = "wide"
)

nepal_born_us <- get_acs_cached(
    "us_nepal_born_acs5",
    geography = "us",
    variables = c(nepal_born = NEPAL_BORN_VAR),
    year = ACS_YEAR, survey = "acs5", output = "wide"
)

us_pct_born_nepal <- nepal_born_us$nepal_bornE / us_pop$nepaleseE

birthplace_top5 <- cbsa_pop |>
    filter(!is.na(nepaleseE)) |>
    slice_max(nepaleseE, n = 5) |>
    left_join(
        nepal_born_cbsa |> select(GEOID, nepal_bornE),
        by = "GEOID"
    ) |>
    mutate(pct_born_nepal = nepal_bornE / nepaleseE)


birthplace_top5 |>
    select(NAME, nepaleseE, nepal_bornE, pct_born_nepal) |>
    gt() |>
    cols_label(NAME = "Metro Area", nepaleseE = "Nepalese (ancestry)",
               nepal_bornE = "Born in Nepal",
               pct_born_nepal = "Born in Nepal (% of Nepalese)") |>
    fmt_number(c(nepaleseE, nepal_bornE), decimals = 0) |>
    fmt_percent(pct_born_nepal, decimals = 0) |>
    tab_header(title = "How Many Nepalese Americans Are Immigrants?",
               subtitle = "ACS 2024 5-year. Approximate: the two tables count people differently.")
```

The birthplace data shows that many people identifying as Nepalese in major US metro areas were born in Nepal. Among the five metro areas analyzed, `r birthplace_top5 |> slice_max(pct_born_nepal, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) |> pull(NAME)` has the highest approximate birthplace ratio at `r scales::percent(max(birthplace_top5$pct_born_nepal, na.rm = TRUE), accuracy = 1)`, while `r birthplace_top5 |> slice_min(pct_born_nepal, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) |> pull(NAME)` has the lowest at `r scales::percent(min(birthplace_top5$pct_born_nepal, na.rm = TRUE), accuracy = 1)`. Nationally, the ratio of Nepal-born residents to people identifying as Nepalese is approximately `r scales::percent(us_pct_born_nepal, accuracy = 0.1)`. These differences suggest that Nepalese communities may have different migration and settlement histories across US cities.


# Neighborhood Income: Nepalese vs. All New Yorkers

```{r}
#| label: ec2-income
# Extra Credit #2b: median household income (B19013_001) by NYC tract.
# Medians can't be added up, so compare the income of the tract the
# typical Nepalese New Yorker lives in vs. the typical New Yorker.
nyc_income <- get_acs_cached(
    "nyc_tracts_income_acs5",
    geography = "tract",
    state     = "NY",
    county    = NYC_COUNTIES,
    variables = c(med_income = "B19013_001"),
    year = ACS_YEAR, survey = "acs5", output = "wide"
)

income_compare <- tract_lookup |>
    left_join(nyc_income |> select(GEOID, med_incomeE), by = "GEOID") |>
    filter(!is.na(med_incomeE))

nepalese_tract_income <- weighted.mean(income_compare$med_incomeE, income_compare$nepalese)
all_tract_income      <- weighted.mean(income_compare$med_incomeE, income_compare$pop)

tibble(
    group  = c("Nepalese New Yorkers", "All New Yorkers"),
    income = c(nepalese_tract_income, all_tract_income)
) |>
    gt() |>
    cols_label(group = "", income = "Median Household Income of Home Tract") |>
    fmt_currency(income, decimals = 0) |>
    tab_header(title = "Neighborhood Income: Nepalese vs. All New Yorkers",
               subtitle = "Population-weighted average of tract medians, ACS 2024 5-year")
```

The income analysis shows that Nepalese New Yorkers live in neighborhoods with an estimated average tract median household income of `r scales::dollar(nepalese_tract_income, accuracy = 1)`, compared with `r scales::dollar(all_tract_income, accuracy = 1)` for New Yorkers overall. This is approximately `r scales::dollar(all_tract_income - nepalese_tract_income, accuracy = 1)` lower, representing a difference of `r scales::percent((all_tract_income - nepalese_tract_income) / all_tract_income, accuracy = 0.1)`. This suggests that Nepalese residents tend to live in neighborhoods with somewhat lower median household incomes than the citywide comparison. However, these figures describe neighborhood income levels, not the actual income of Nepalese households.

## Atlas Entry

### A Little Nepal in New York City

New York City has become an important home for Nepalese Americans, especially in Queens. Neighborhoods such as Jackson Heights and Elmhurst are known for their South Asian communities, where visitors can find Nepali restaurants, grocery stores, and businesses that reflect the community's culture.

According to the 2024 ACS 5-year estimates, `r nta_data |> filter(NTAType == 0) |> st_drop_geometry() |> slice_max(nepalese, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) |> pull(NTAName)` has the largest estimated Nepalese population among NYC's residential Neighborhood Tabulation Areas, with approximately `r nta_data |> filter(NTAType == 0) |> st_drop_geometry() |> summarize(n = max(nepalese, na.rm = TRUE)) |> pull(n) |> scales::comma()` residents identifying as Nepalese. The interactive NYC map below helps show how the community is distributed across different neighborhoods.

```{r}
#| label: fig-map-nyc-nepalese
# Extra Credit #1: interactive map + bar chart linked by data_id.
# Hovering a neighborhood in either panel highlights it in both.
library(ggiraph)
library(patchwork)

nta_res <- nta_data |>
    filter(NTAType == 0) |>
    mutate(tooltip = paste0(NTAName, " (", BoroName, ")\n",
                            comma(nepalese), " Nepalese residents\n",
                            percent(nepalese_share, 0.1), " of neighborhood"))

nyc_map <- ggplot(nta_res) +
    geom_sf_interactive(aes(fill = nepalese_share, tooltip = tooltip,
                            data_id = NTA2020),
                        color = "white", linewidth = 0.1) +
    geom_sf(data = nta_data |> filter(NTAType != 0),
            fill = "grey90", color = "white", linewidth = 0.1) +
    scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "magma", direction = -1,
                         labels = percent, name = "Nepalese\nshare") +
    theme_void()

top_ntas <- nta_res |>
    st_drop_geometry() |>
    slice_max(nepalese, n = 15)

nyc_bars <- ggplot(top_ntas,
                   aes(x = nepalese, y = fct_reorder(NTAName, nepalese))) +
    geom_col_interactive(aes(tooltip = tooltip, data_id = NTA2020),
                         fill = "#7a2048") +
    scale_x_continuous(labels = comma) +
    labs(x = "Nepalese residents", y = NULL) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 9)

girafe(
    ggobj = (nyc_map | nyc_bars) +
        plot_layout(widths = c(1.3, 1)) +
        plot_annotation(
            title    = "Nepalese Residents by NYC Neighborhood",
            subtitle = "ACS 2024 5-year; hover to compare. Grey = parks, airports, cemeteries"
        ),
    width_svg = 10, height_svg = 5.5,
    options = list(
        opts_hover(css = "stroke:black;stroke-width:1.5px;"),
        opts_hover_inv(css = "opacity:0.35;"),
        opts_tooltip(css = "background:white;color:black;padding:6px;border-radius:4px;font-size:12px;")
    )
)
```

### Beyond New York: Nepalese Communities Across America

Although New York City is an important center for Nepalese Americans, the community extends well beyond the city. According to the 2024 ACS 5-year estimates, approximately `r scales::comma(us_nepalese)` people across the United States identify as Nepalese. The New York metropolitan area accounts for about `r scales::percent(ny_share, accuracy = 0.1)` of this population, while the ten metro areas with the largest Nepalese populations together account for `r scales::percent(top10_share, accuracy = 0.1)`.

One interesting finding is the presence of a large Nepalese community in the Dallas metropolitan area, showing that Nepalese settlement is not limited to traditional immigrant destinations like New York. Opportunities for employment, education, and family connections may help explain why Nepalese communities have developed in different parts of the country.

The interactive US map below shows these patterns, with larger circles representing metro areas with more Nepalese residents. Readers can hover over each circle to explore the estimated population.

```{r}
#| label: fig-map-us-metros
# Metro shapes (cached) + state outlines, with Alaska/Hawaii moved under the map
cbsa_geo <- get_acs_cached(
    "cbsa_nepalese_acs5_geom",
    geography = "cbsa",
    variables = c(total = "B01003_001", nepalese = GROUP_VAR),
    year      = ACS_YEAR,
    survey    = "acs5",
    output    = "wide",
    geometry  = TRUE
) |>
    filter(!str_detect(NAME, ", PR"), !is.na(nepaleseE), nepaleseE > 0) |>
    tigris::shift_geometry() |>
    st_centroid()

us_states <- tigris::states(cb = TRUE, resolution = "20m", year = ACS_YEAR) |>
    filter(!STUSPS %in% c("PR", "VI", "GU", "MP", "AS")) |>
    tigris::shift_geometry()

cbsa_geo <- cbsa_geo |>
    arrange(desc(nepaleseE)) |>   # big bubbles drawn first, small ones on top
    mutate(tooltip = paste0(NAME, "\n", comma(nepaleseE),
                            " Nepalese residents (±", comma(nepaleseM), ")"))

us_map <- ggplot() +
    geom_sf(data = us_states, fill = "grey95", color = "white") +
    geom_sf_interactive(data = cbsa_geo,
                        aes(size = nepaleseE, tooltip = tooltip, data_id = GEOID),
                        color = "#d1495b", alpha = 0.6) +
    scale_size_area(max_size = 14, labels = comma, name = "Nepalese\nresidents") +
    labs(title = "Where Nepalese Americans Live",
         subtitle = "Metro areas, ACS 2024 5-year; hover a bubble for details") +
    theme_void()

girafe(
    ggobj = us_map,
    width_svg = 10, height_svg = 6,
    options = list(
        opts_hover(css = "fill:#7a2048;stroke:black;"),
        opts_tooltip(css = "background:white;color:black;padding:6px;border-radius:4px;font-size:12px;")
    )
)
```


### From Nepal to America: A Story of Migration

Nepalese migration to the United States was relatively small before the 2000s but grew significantly in the following decades. Many Nepalese people moved to America in search of education, employment, and better opportunities. According to a [2024 study published in *Genealogy*](https://www.mdpi.com/2313-5778/8/2/42), Nepalese immigration increased considerably after 2000, helping communities develop in different parts of the country.

Another important chapter began in 2008, when Bhutanese refugees who had been living in camps in Nepal started arriving in the United States through resettlement programs. As reported by the [United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR)](https://www.unhcr.org/news/briefing-notes/nepal-large-scale-resettlement-refugees-bhutan), many of these refugees had spent years in Nepal before moving abroad. Although many shared Nepalese language and cultural traditions, they originally came from Bhutan. 

The 2015 earthquake in Nepal also affected Nepalese communities in America. Following the disaster, the [US Department of Homeland Security](https://www.govinfo.gov/app/details/FR-2015-06-24/2015-15576) designated Nepal for Temporary Protected Status (TPS), allowing eligible Nepalese nationals already living in the United States to remain and work temporarily.
